anatomy.intro: Glossy cupped leaves, short stalks, fleshy branches, and slender flower spikes make up this compact plant.

parts.function: The fleshy blade stores moisture and has a recessed midrib running toward its rounded tip.
parts.label: Thick leaf

parts.function: A short stalk attaches the leaf blade to the stem.
parts.label: Petiole

parts.function: Fleshy stems carry successive leaves and give the plant its bushy form.
parts.label: Branching stem

parts.function: Many tiny petal-less flowers crowd onto a slender upright axis.
parts.label: Flower spike

flowers.text: A cream-white spike about 3.5–5 inches long holds many minute flowers. Each flower has two stamens and no petals, creating a narrow, grainy-looking surface instead of a showy bloom.

growth.note: Softwood stem cuttings can root in free-draining medium or water before potting. NC State also lists leaf cuttings for the species; allow this recently purchased plant to establish first.

stages.text: Small leaves expand along growing shoots, gradually revealing their cupped shape and cream-green pattern.
stages.title: New leafy shoots

stages.text: Side branches fill out the canopy; compare new stem spacing with older growth when reviewing light.
stages.title: Branching clump

stages.text: Slender spikes can develop without the showy petals of many other houseplants.
stages.title: Flower spikes

habitat.text: The species belongs to tropical America; the named Bicolor cultivar has a horticultural origin. A Veracruz field study records Peperomia obtusifolia growing on trees, on the ground, and on rock across several forest types, including humid and seasonally drier forests. Thick leaves therefore do not make this plant a desert specialist.

lookalikes.name: Rubber plant, Ficus elastica
lookalikes.text: Both have glossy thick leaves, but Ficus forms a woody tree with much larger leathery blades. Peperomia's compact fleshy stems and slender flower spikes distinguish the baby rubber plant; the common name does not indicate close relationship.

mature.text: The species forms a rounded, branching herbaceous plant about 6 inches to 2 feet in height and spread. Fleshy stems and broad leaves create fullness without the woody trunk of a true rubber tree.

milestones.text: Purchased at Carlson's Greenhouses in a reported six-inch nursery basket; the tag supplies the Bicolor name.
milestones.title: Purchased and labeled

milestones.title: Living-room layout planned

nameStory.text: The Obtipan breeder record describes a cross between two unnamed Peperomia obtusifolia cultivars. RHS lists Obtipan Bicolor separately. The species belongs to the pepper family, while its baby rubber plant nickname describes the thick leaves.

sources.title: Vergara-Rodríguez et al.: Peperomia diversity and ecology in Veracruz
